At four metres the lamp stopped being a lamp, so Vance put it out. Charge spent to light her
own glove is charge, and she had eleven metres to cross and a way back to think about.

She went on the count. The intakes sat low and steady off her right shoulder where they
belonged. The current off the exchangers carried her a little to the left, the way it always
carried. At ten she put her hand out early, because she always put her hand out early, and
at eleven the yoke came up cold under her palm and rang once and stopped.

"Cradle," she said. "Hand on it."

The wire took a moment.

"You are not slotted," Quiej said.

"No."

"I am not asking you a question. I am telling you that I have logged the answer."

"Log it," Vance said, and went to work.

She started at the deep end of the yoke and went along it with the flat of her hand. Bolt.
Bolt. The welt of the old repair, which was rougher than it had been and which she would
think about later. Bolt. The core sat in the cradle the way it had sat since the
fire, and whether it sat there another day or another decade depended entirely on people who
had never put a hand on it.

She got a thumb around what she could reach of the seal ring and found nothing under it,
which meant nothing. A hairline is under a thumb and always will be. The sonar would not tell
her either; it would give her the shape of the ring and say not one word about its condition.
Those two facts together were most of what her work had become.

Then in under the lip, behind the yoke, where the drawing said there was nothing at all, she
found the seating.

It was not where the paper put it. It was two fingers lower and turned a little out of true,
and when she had it she understood that whoever seated it had known exactly where it was,
and that the knowing had never been written anywhere the co-op could be made to produce.

The seating was a cup, and a collar, and a slot her fingers said was empty.

Empty of what, she could not say. She went round it twice. The cup was clean and the collar
turned under her thumb the way a collar that has been maintained turns, and the slot was
sized for something she had never held, and whatever belonged in it was not in it now and
might not have been in it since the day they capped the shaft. She had come down for a fact and what she had was a
shape.

Thirty years of co-op paper and not one line of it says where the readkey went.

"Say what you have," the wire said.

"I have the seating."

"Is the read-key in it?"

She held her palm flat against the collar as if it might answer. Steel at four degrees takes
the heat out of a hand in about a minute, and she gave it the minute.

"There is a slot," she said. "The slot is empty. I cannot tell you whether it was ever full."

"Then you have nothing, and you have it without a slot on the board. Come up."

"Trust me," she told the wire, and heard exactly how it sounded.

It sounded like a woman in the dark with her hand on a thing she could not name, asking to
be believed. She had gone her whole working life without that sentence and there had been a
reason for it. In the water it is what people say when they have run out of procedure.

Quiej let it stand. That was worse than an argument, and both of them knew it.

"Coming up," Vance said.

"I have logged that too."

She did not move yet. She put both hands on the seating and held them there, the way she had
been taught to hold a thing she was going to have to describe from memory, and she went over
it once more, and it told her exactly as much the second time as the first. Shape and no name. Somewhere above her the shelf worked and the cradle took
the note and held it, and the note went up through her wrists and into her teeth and ran out.

There was one pair of hands on Nix that would know what belonged in that slot. They were not
hands that could be asked. The rest of him had been emptied out on a form he signed on the
deck of a lock, and she had spent every hour since telling herself that a thing taken can be
got back if you are stubborn enough about it, and down here, with the collar turning clean
and empty under her thumb, that stopped being something she could say to herself.

She could go up with this. She could go up with the shape of it and a drawing that was wrong
and a slot the co-op would tell her had always been empty, and the board would thank her for
her time.

Or she could ask her brother.

She let go of the cradle and turned, and the dark did not change when she turned, because it
had nothing to change from. Eleven metres. The intakes off her left shoulder now. The current
pushing her back the way it had carried her out, which was the one piece of charity in the
whole room.

At four metres from the throat she still could not see the throat.

She put her hand out early.
